newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-BSkyB throws German digital TV into disarray.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-BSkyB throws German digital TV into disarray.

text.p: Germany's fledgling digital pay television industry was thrown into disarray on Friday after British Sky Broadcasting (BSkyB) said it had pulled out of a joint venture with Leo Kirch's DF1 channel.
The announcement was a major setback for the Bavarian media mogul, who has recently lost a court case against rival pay TV group Premiere and has attracted fewer than 30,000 subscribers to DF1.

"Kirch Group and British Sky Broadcasting have cancelled their agreement for a partnership in the digital platform of DF1 because of a failure to agree a number of fundamental issues," the two companies said in a joint statement announcing the rupture.

BSkyB, whose largest shareholder is media tycoon Rupert Murdoch's News News Corp, had planned to take a 49 percent stake in DF1, but the talks dragged on and six weeks ago the British firm said contracts had not been finalised.
Gottfried Zmeck, a senior Kirch Group official, said there were "interested parties" ready to talk about taking BSkyB's place.
"We are open for a partner, but this is not an existential question," Zmeck said.

DF1 spokesman Nikolaus von der Decken said the collapse of the partnership with BSkyB also meant the British satellite broadcaster would not take a stake in DSF, an all-sports channel in which Kirch is a major shareholder.

DF1's rival Premiere is Germany's only analogue pay TV channel and has more than 1.4 million subscribers. It is owned by media giant Bertelsmann AG, French pay TV group Canal Plus and Kirch, who has a minority shareholding.
Frustrated with the lack of control over Premiere, Kirch set out last year on his own to establish a competing pay TV company for digital broadcasting services.

There has been speculation that Canal Plus could sell Kirch its stake in Premiere in exchange for Kirch's stake in Telepiu, an Italian pay TV group. Bertelsmann officials say this is not likely to happen and say they could veto any such move.

Digital technology allows broadcasters to squeeze more channels into cable and satellite networks and to show films in CD-like quality. It also allows new media forms such as video on demand, home-shopping and possibly interactive games.

Germany is Europe's biggest media market and foreign broadcasters are keen to get a foot in the door. But there are also digital TV projects up and running in other countries such as France and Italy.
DF1 faced significant hurdles even before it could get off the ground and fell short of its original goal of attaining 200,000 subscribers last year.
Premiere has frustrated Kirch's efforts with a string of court challenges.

DF1 has also had difficulty obtaining subscribers because it is restricted to broadcasting via satellite as it has not yet reached an agreement with Deutsche Telekom to distribute the service on the phone company's cable television network.
The majority of Germans receive television programming from cable rather than satellite.
"We are still negotiating. There have been no new developments," a Telekom spokesman said.

Earlier this week, Premiere warned that the entire digital pay TV industry in Germany could fail unless DF1 and Premiere reached some form of agreement to integrate the two services, sharing DF1's digital platform and Premiere's customers.
Premiere has launched a digital pilot project with some 30,000 of its subscribers and believes that thousands more would be willing to trade their analogue service for digital services.
-- Bonn Newsroom, 49 228 26097150
